896 7735 6598 Passcode: 036922 (Please note you will not have the ability to speak using the call-in option from

-  Public  correspondence  may  be  emailed  to  Carol  Corea, Administrative Assistant at
carolc@rollinghillsestatesca.gov. Emails received before 5:00 p.m. the night of the meeting will be forwarded to

public, will be considered by the Committee and become part of the record.

- Members of the public who join the Zoom meeting will not have video and may request to speak using the

Agenda reports and other disclosable public records relating to each agenda item are available on the City's
website under Meeting Agendas, Minutes & Videos at www.rhe.city/agendas.

MINUTES
  ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  OCTOBER 27, 2021

CHAIR STEGURA called the meeting of the Environmental Advisory Committee of the City of
Rolling Hills Estates to order at 7:00 p.m.

2.  ROLL CALL

COMMITTEE MEMBERS PRESENT:  Stegura, Bacinski, Bain, Chan-Southwell,
  Radocchio, Uppal, Wisot

COMMITTEE MEMBERS ABSENT:  Larson, O’Malley, Schachter, Yoo

STAFF MEMBERS PRESENT:  Alexa Davis, Assistant City Manager
  Jeannie Naughton, Planning Manager
  Levi Sinkler, Administrative Aide
  Carol Corea, Administrative Assistant

ALSO PRESENT:  Tammie Myers, California Water Service
  Angie Gilbride, California Water Service
  Agustin Beeza, California Water Service

3.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

A.  APPROVAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING, JUNE 16,
  2021

COMMITTEE MEMBER WISOT made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER
RADOCCHIO to,

  APPROVE THE ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING MINUTES OF
  JUNE 16, 2021

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

4.  AUDIENCE ITEMS/ORAL COMMUNICATION ON ITEMS NOT ON THE AGENDA

NONE

5.  DISCUSSION ITEMS

A.  SCE CHARGE READY 2 PROGRAM UPDATE

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that there were two different programs discussed at the last
meeting. The City already has the grant for the SCAQMD project, which was approved in 2018;
however, there were delays due to COVID and staff was looking for opportunities to leverage and
evaluate different sites. There will be two dual port stations at Ernie Howlett park and staff is
working on securing proposals/quotes for the infrastructure, station, and ADA improvements
needed. These quotes will come back to the EAC for review at a future meeting.

Administrative Aide Sinkler stated that at their meeting in June 2021, the EAC provided guidance
for the SCE Charge Ready 2 Program. The City has been approved for twelve ports at the City
Hall location. Staff is seeking direction from the EAC on whether to move forward with installation.
An overview of the program requirements was provided. The Highridge Park location was denied;
however, SCE informed staff that if the City were to propose sixteen ports, they could proceed
with the project. Staff has reached out to two station providers – Charge Point, which is the city’s
current station provider, and EV Connect. The quote from Charge Point was $73,850 and the
quote from EV Connect was $71,250, both of which includes the installation and a five-year labor
and maintenance warranty. Staff has also been exploring the cost of only the installation with a
contractor the city has used in the past. With these costs, the City is eligible for a $725 per port
rebate from SCE, which accounts for approximately $8,700.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  1
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 27, 2021
 Administrative Aide Sinkler stated that staff recommends that the Environmental Advisory
Committee recommend that the City proceed with the SCE Charge Ready 2 program and enter
into agreement with SCE for the infrastructure buildout and installation of six (6) dual port charging
stations at City Hall for the future consideration and approval by the City Council.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI inquired about any data on expected usage. Assistant City
Manager Davis stated that staff has the current station data, and it is actively used, however,
there needs to be a restructuring of the rates for the charging station. This is part of the City’s
Sustainability Element with the goal of increasing EV infrastructure and understanding that there
will be a ban on fossil fuel vehicles by 2035. This provides a proactive approach to building
infrastructure and utilizing available grant money and taking advantage of programs for this
purpose.

COMMITTEE MEMBER RADOCCHIO asked if the two station providers provided a breakdown
to account for the difference in cost. Administrative Aide Sinkler stated that they did provide an
itemized breakdown, but staff cannot disclose this due to competitive reasons.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN inquired if charging station providers, such as Charge Point, rebate
any portion of the fees that are collected to the hosting site. She also inquired if the City will have
any revenue stream from the twelve ports. Administrative Aide Sinkler stated that there are no
restrictions on the pricing structure that the City can use. Assistant City Manager Davis stated
that the current station was established to be revenue neutral. Staff will be bringing an updated
review of the rates to the EAC within the next year.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that the staff report notes that this was not in the budget for this year,
but park facility fees may be able to be used and asked for the best highest use for the twelve
ports next to City Hall that benefit all the auxiliary activities. Assistant City Manager Davis stated
that the current station was funded using park facility fees. City Hall is used for public restrooms
and the Chamber is used for community meetings. COMMITTEE MEMBER STEGURA added
that high usage could also be expected from people using the riding ring next to City Hall,
Chandler Park and people using Seahorse riding ring.

CHAIR STEGURA asked if a gas-powered vehicle is allowed to park in EV charging parking
spaces. Administrative Aide Sinkler stated that there is nothing prohibiting a internal combustion
engine vehicle from parking in these spaces. There would need to be a resolution or ordinance
established by the City prohibiting this. CHAIR STEGURA stated that this might be an issue if
charging stations were installed at Highridge Park since there are fewer parking spaces. Assistant
City Manager Davis stated that staff was also concerned with the impact to available parking
spaces for non-EV users. In this case, staff would want to do a study of how many electric vehicles
are coming in and out.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI asked about time limits for internal combustion engines.
Assistant City Manager Davis stated that it would be an enforcement issue, however, time limits
for electric vehicles would be a matter of having a time limit on the charging station.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked if there is data on how long vehicles are parking at the City
Hall spaces. Assistant City Manager Davis stated that staff can access this data from the current
station provider dashboard. Administrative Aide Sinkler stated that from the last quarterly report,
the average session was 4.3 hours. The typical charge time for a Level Two charger may take a
full day, depending on the battery size.

COMMITTEE MEMBER UPPAL stated that she does like that there is no time restriction, and it
typically takes about four hours for a full charge.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked if SCE is sharing any information on any changes in
technology where these stations would need to be replaced in a few years or even become
obsolete; the city should be ready for any changes coming up. Administrative Aide Sinkler stated
that he has not heard of any changes, but under the agreement with SCE, these chargers need
to be maintained for ten years. Staff will explore any upcoming changes and their capability.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked about data from other cities on the repair cost and any
problems to anticipate. Assistant City Manager Davis stated that we do not have data from other
cities, but staff can reach out to Torrance for any data. For the current station at the city, all repairs
and a technical upgrade have been covered under the warranty plan.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER RADOCCHIO to,

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  2
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 27, 2021
   RECOMMEND THAT THE CITY PROCEED WITH THE SCE CHARGE READY 2
  PROGRAM AND ENTER INTO AGREEMENT WITH SCE FOR THE INFRASTRUCTURE
  BUILDOUT AND INSTALLATION OF SIX (6) DUAL PORT CHARGING STATIONS AT
  CITY HALL FOR THE FUTURE CONSIDERATION AND APPROVAL BY THE CITY
  COUNCIL.

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

B.  AQMD-MSRC GRANT - ZERO EMISSION VEHICLE PROCUREMENT

Administrative Aide Sinkler stated that staff is requesting that the EAC consider the procurement
of one zero emission vehicle utilizing the SCAQMD reimbursable grant funds. In 2018, the City
was awarded matching grant funding totaling $10,000 by SCAQMD towards the purchase of a
light duty zero emission vehicle. The vehicle recommended for purchase is the 2022 Volt EV with
a cost of $30,073. It would be used by all eligible staff conducting city business during city hours.
The city has budgeted for this vehicle purchase.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI inquired about the cost of insurance. Assistant City Manager
Davis stated that the City is self-insured and this should not affect the overall insurance cost with
the city’s equipment program.

In response to a question by CHAIR STEGURA, Assistant City Manager Davis stated that priority
for use of the vehicle would be given to Code Enforcement and Traffic Control and staff will
continue to look for grant opportunities to purchase more vehicles in the future.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked if there is an option to buy a used vehicle with low miles and
if National Auto Fleet is the only vendor the city can use. Administrative Aide Sinkler that this
vendor provided the best price being 6% under MSRP. Staff explored used vehicles, but the city
needs to maintain the vehicle for three years; there is a risk with used vehicles that the battery
may go out. COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN stated that she believes electric vehicles sold in the
State of California come with a 150K mile warranty and electric vehicles have better maintenance
records than regular vehicles.

COMMITTEE MEMBER STEGURA asked what determined the choice for a Volt and if there are
any recalls. Administrative Aide Sinkler stated that staff was informed that any recalls would be
resolved by the vehicle delivery time. The other two vehicles that staff looked into were a higher
cost.

COMMITTEE MEMBER WISOT made a motion, seconded by COMMITTEE MEMBER
RADOCCHIO to,

  RECOMMEND TO THE CITY COUNCIL TO PROCEED WITH THE PROCUREMENT OF
  THE 2022 CHEVROLET BOLT EV 5DR WAGON 1LT.

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA so ordered.

C.  ASSEMBLY BILL (AB) 1346 - AIR POLLUTION: SMALL OFF-ROAD ENGINES

Planning Manager Naughton stated that this was explored previously in relation to gas leaf
blowers; in terms of decibel levels, electric leaf blowers have a high decibel level but is at a
different frequency, however, they are still quite noisy.

Assembly Bill (AB) 1346 was signed into law earlier this month and this will phase out the sale of
Small Off-Road Engines (SORE). This is primarily lawn and garden equipment, but also includes
construction, farming and airport equipment. The bill is requiring that the California Air Resources
Board (CARB) come up with emission requirements for these SORE to zero by 2024 or when
CARB determines is feasible.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that she has not been able to find data on the timeline for
adopting the new emission standards. The bill also requires that CARB identify and to the extent
feasible, provide funding for commercial rebates and for similar incentive funding programs as
part of any updates to program guidelines to local districts. The Assemblymembers who
introduced the bill, Marc Berman and Lorena Gonzalez, have secured $30M in the State’s budget
this year to create a statewide incentive program to businesses transition to zero emission
equipment.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  3
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 27, 2021
 Planning Manager Naughton stated that included with the staff report was the op-ed which does
a great job of seeing the issue from both sides – how this will affect small businesses to transition
to zero emission and the health and environmental effects of SORE.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that she will continue to monitor the status of CARB emission
setting regulations and bring information back to the EAC.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked how the $30M will be used. Planning Manager Naughton
stated that it looks like the funding is going to go to the local Air Quality Management Districts.
SCAQMD would obtain a portion of that and implement a grant program.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN stated that her gardener purchased an electric leaf blower at a
significant discount and was not sure how he received the discount. She inquired if the City could
look into any programs apart from the $30M to incentivize people to transition to this equipment.
Planning Manager Naughton stated that the SCAQMD currently has a commercial lawn and
garden program, but it is limited; hopefully, the additional money may be able to expand the
program. The City would need to look for grants that may be able to supplement the SCAQMD
programs. Planning Manager Naughton stated that one of the challenges is recharging and there
may be opportunity to not only expand vehicle charging infrastructure but also infrastructure for
charging batteries for small off-road engines.

COMMITTEE MEMBER STEGURA stated that much like the organic waste program, the City can
begin to educate the community on this upcoming change.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN stated that her gardener was not so much concerned with the
environmental effects but the cost of gas, but it’s the only way he can work quickly. The small
business owners will need support from the community to make this transition. The entire
Peninsula should move towards a program to help these small businesses to transition.

There being no objection, CHAIR STEGURA moved to receive and file this item.

D.  STATEWIDE DROUGHT EMERGENCY AND CONSERVATION MEASURES (VERBAL
  REPORT

Planning Manager Naughton stated that in July 2021, the Governor issued an executive order
asking for a voluntary 15% reduction of water use in California and signed a proclamation of a
state of emergency of water shortage in many counties in the State. In October 2021, he included
Los Angeles County in an updated state of emergency proclamation.

CHAIR STEGURA stated that in the past the EAC recommended to the Council to invoke
emergency water conservation measures that are already provided for in the Municipal Code.

Planning Manager Naughton introduced Tammie Myers, Conservation Coordinator with California
Water Service, who provided a presentation to the EAC. Ms. Myers stated that CalWater is
working to help educate and notify residents and constituents about water conservation.

Ms. Myers provided an overview of their Conservation webpage (CalWater.com/conservation)
and access to the various resources. In addition, information was provided on their water
efficiency programs. An explanation of the Lawn-to-Garden rebate program was explained
including an example of what the rebate would look like in order to remove the lawn in front of
City Hall.

COMMITTEE MEMBER BACINSKI asked about how this information is being publicized. Ms.
Myers stated that they are ramping up their marketing and outreach with social media, radio and
television ads.

PLANNING MANAGER NAUGHTON asked if there is any data available on the water savings
using the City Hall example. Ms. Myers stated that she could provide this and explained that some
variables would need to be factored in in order to provide an estimate.

Ms. Myers provided the overall water savings on the Peninsula for residents who have utilized
their conservation programs.

CHAIR STEGURA thanked Ms. Myers and stated that the City should also include this information
in their media.

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  4
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 27, 2021
 COMMITTEE MEMBER BAIN asked if these programs could be used for the City Parks to see
what parts would be amenable to different landscape design. Ms. Myers stated that this could
definitely be done.

Assistant City Manager Davis stated that she is in contact with Ms. Myers to coordinate a meeting
on a water audit on the City’s water usage. This information should be coming forward to the EAC,
Parks and Activities Commission and City Council.

6.  MANAGER ITEMS

Planning Manager Naughton stated that the draft Sustainability Element will be presented to the
EAC at the next meeting. Staff will send an email poll to the committee to schedule the next
meeting date.

Planning Manager Naughton stated that there is a Special Joint City Council and Planning
Commission meeting on Tuesday, November 9th at 5:00 p.m. that will focus on the Program
Environmental Impact Report and an overview of the General Plan chapters. The comment period
for the EIR ends on December 6th. The first Public Hearing meeting with the Planning Commission
is also scheduled on December 6th. There will be no decision on the General Plan, this is an
introduction to the Planning Commission on the EIR and to the General Plan. The next meeting
is anticipated to be on January 10th, which at that time the Planning Commission may have a
recommendation to move forward to the City Council. Staff would like the EAC to have time to
review the draft Sustainability Element and provide recommendations to the Planning
Commission prior to the January 10th meeting.

7.  COMMITTEE ITEMS/FUTURE AGENDA ITEMS

NONE

8.  ADJOURNMENT

CHAIR STEGURA adjourned the meeting at 8:26 p.m.

Submitted by,  Approved by,

_____________________________  ____________________________
Carol Corea, Administrative Assistant  Debby Stegura, Chair

 ENVIRONMENTAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE MEETING
  5
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 27, 2021
